Broadcasting multicast services via beamforming networks offers an efficient method to enhance spectral efficacy and data throughput. Nevertheless, implementing traditional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) multicast streams remains restricted due to prevalent hardware constraints, such as the scarcity of radio frequency (RF) chains and non-orthogonal physical layer resources. To address these limitations, hybrid beamforming presents an optimal framework for leveraging mmWave capabilities. While research has established theoretical frameworks for optimizing digital and analog precoders using minimum mean-squared error (MSE) criteria in multicast networks, practical enforcement is hindered by intense computational complexity and reliance on precise channel state information regarding both transmitter and receiver environments. Consequently, we introduce a streamlined algorithm based on Gaussian quadrature that reduces computational overhead and requires fewer resources compared to existing methods. This proposed technique successfully achieves performance nearly on a par with state-of-the-art solutions while supporting systems with limited hardware capacity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that reducing the amount of available hardware materially impacts computational complexity but concurrently degrades overall system capacity and performance.

Communication bottlenecks remain a persistent obstacle within the federated learning framework. To address this, we introduce Communication-Efficient Federated Distillation (CEFD), a novel framework designed federal communication scenarios. By employing a process of knowledge distillation, we reduce the transmissions between clients and the central server. Specifically, we transform the federated learning task into an optimization strategy, replacing standard parameter-updating client uploads with distilled knowledge representations that facilitate streamlined communications. To further lessen data exchange volumes, we incorporate quantization techniques on these distilled representations. Additionally, communication bandwidth constraints are mitigated by leveraging simulated aggregation responses rather than actual server feedback. Comprehensive experiments utilizing the non-IID distributed MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method lowers inter-client-and-server communication costs by as much as 90% without substantial sacrifices in model accuracy.

Current multi-objective optimization approaches typically rely on a predefined utility function provided by experts. However, acquiring accurate utility functions presents significant challenges in practical scenarios. Simultaneously, existing automated methods typically ignore pre-existing expert or past knowledge and exhibit poor sample efficiency. To address these limitations, this study presents Kachey, a differential equations-based framework that efficiently learns utility functions by integrating both past experience and domain-specific expert knowledge. The system models the utility function as a dynamic, time-varying process where historical data helps estimate initial conditions, while expert insights inform the differential equations governing its evolution. Correspondingly, we have developed two new methods: one integrates Bayesian priors from the system's state-space into the utility function model to reduce sampling needs, whereas the other employs knowledge distillation to leverage and generalize lessons learned from multiple tasks. Experimental validation confirms that our approach markedly lowers sampling requirements and substantially enhances performance compared to existing methods.

This research focuses on a core dilemma in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL): whether to employ time-homogeneous models even in scenarios involving significant non-stationarities or shifts. When non-stochastic changes occur, model-based risk-sensitive algorithms achieve optimal performance only by utilizing fully adaptive methods that dynamically select between homogeneous and non-homogeneous policies based on change frequency. Previous approaches, however, impose strictly linear cost functions—a rigid constraint this work breaks. By introducing a more intricate and interpretation-appropriate risk-sensitive cost framework—encompassing functions like Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk—we demonstrate a groundbreaking separation mechanism for detecting non-stationarities. Our proposed algorithm, CL-RS-AD-Ri, offers near-optimal performance and delivers an adaptive guarantee designed to accommodate these specific, non-linear cost structures.

Organizations utilize public instances of the collaborative issue-tracking platform, Jira, to maintain communication regarding the progress of their products and services on the internet. However, public Jira repositories are currently underutilized; available data consists of fewer than 100 repositories, which is significantly fewer than the hundreds of GitHub repositories found on similar platforms. In addition, in order to facilitate the exploration and analysis of similar datasets by the broader community, we will present the dataset publicly.

Current CTR forecasting for advertisements with limited recent impression data typically functions as conventional advertising, utilizing pre-trained models that do not account for individual ad uniqueness. First, we redefine the factor graph by separating outlier detection from noise modeling into distinct nodes; accordingly, our message passing steps are split accordingly to process information through separate paths. Second, our approach employs cyclic check-scheduling to ensure stable operation. Simulation comparisons demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over both the standard PDA and a robust Kalman Filter variant, specifically regarding robustness and computational efficiency.

This paper demonstrates that under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for certain eighth-degree L-functions, the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is bounded. Our approach employs Watson's formula to reformulate the original problem as a moment issue concerning L-functions, thereby enabling the application of Sharp-bound techniques previously developed by Soundararajan and Harper for the moments of the Riemann zeta function.

In interior point methods (IPMs), iterative schemes for solving linear systems typically prioritize acceleration through carefully chosen preconditioners. While highly effective in iterative IPMs, these preconditioners are generally useless for standard IPMs, as their approximations compromise solution accuracy and optimality. Although some nonpreconditioned iterative IPMs exist, they often exhibit sensitivity to the affine representation of feasible regions. This paper introduces a strategy integrating an iterative solver with modified stopping criteria specifically for interior point optimization. By applying appropriate stopping criteria, this approach achieves solutions that are both more precise and less sensitive to directional biases. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that utilizing this novel criterion can substantially boost computational performance when implemented within dual potential reduction methods.

The polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ is explicitly derived up to 3-loop order using the Larin scheme and is valid for all values of the Mellin variable $N$ under both double- and single-quark mass conditions. This component serves an operational function within the three-loop variable flavor number scheme. In the context of perturbation theory, the result is expressed continuously across different ranges of $N$ via its representation in mixed Landau pole $\alpha_s$ and massive factorization schemes, which can then be transformed into the specific domain of the variable flavor number scheme.

Established industries like aviation leverage real-world incidents within centralized databases to enhance safety, yet AI-intelligent systems currently inflict real world damage with 35% security vulnerabilities remaining unfixed at the time of deployment. Consequently, we introduced the AI Incident Database and API, a novel resource designed to help industry leaders learn from past errors. This API ingested 230 AI incident reports from global sources containing complete narratives of incidents along with their origins and consequences through 2021.

After analyzing the data through the lens of our industry-standard AI safety classifications, we found that 62.5% of incidents involved self-driving vehicles and 37.5% stemmed from deceptive AI. Furthermore, 50% of these cases represented repeat incidents. Finally, the provided documentation and analysis support continued efforts to develop responsible AI technologies.

Traditional process monitoring has primarily tracked execution against a single process model and has not often accommodated multiple simultaneous specifications, which may include procedural definitions, data constraints, or machine learning algorithms. While some existing techniques handle conflicts by specifying a global priority hierarchy to determine validity, we explore more nuanced strategies for resolving discrepancies, particularly non-prospective monitoring scenarios where all rules remain potentially relevant. In this paper, we investigate how to manage conflicts by categorizing them based on their source, designed various monitoring algorithms for different specification combinations, and evaluate their efficacy through experiments with executed hybri d executions against a real-word business process specification derived from VAEs.

We investigate a system where a long-lived two-level atom, serving as a nonlinear component, couples to a optical resonator. We demonstrate that this interaction facilitates a unique form of bosonic pair generation involving the simultaneous amplification of the intracavity field and the coherent, collective coupling of multiple atoms (superradiance). Because this process hinges on the nonlinearity arising from the atomic population's collective behavior, it theoretically enables quantum radiation pressure interactions between photons and atomic spin excitations. We further explore how these dynamics facilitate continuous-variable quantum information processing, specifically achieving nearly unity efficiency in measuring the atomic collective phase through an adapted two-stage protocol. This approach theoretically achieves cavity-mediated coupling strengths of approximately 1 Hz and predicts an achievable phase sensitivity of 0.001 radians involving a ten-atom ensemble.

De novo genome assembly involves reconstructing an entire, unknown genome from a vast collection of overlapping short reads, an increasingly vital process in biological research with applications ranging from clinical diagnostics to studying species biodiversity. While assembling long sequencing reads offers distinct challenges, they provide the advantage of more complete contigs and fewer gaps than short reads. Contemporary contig-generation algorithms rely on a "k-mer" strategy, constructing a graph of local read overlaps and extracting linear sequences from isolated clusters. However, assembling contemporary large genomes with this approach generates massive numbers of distinct local connections, resulting in memory requirements far exceeding the capacity of single modern machines. Furthermore, developing efficient serial or single-machine parallel systems using transformative new long read data proves too slow or non-scalable to handle the volume of modern datasets. Conventional heuristic methods also struggle to preserve data integrity as they delete critical overlaps to reduce the size of the assembly graph. We present a distributed-memory algorithm designed to address these challenges, enabling the parallel construction of the genome length-based local overlap structure on long sequences in a way that uses memory-efficient mechanisms and scalable network protocols. The performance evaluation of this method demonstrates that the system can process the read data from even some of the world's most massive next-generation sequencing projects in a high-performance environment, specifically allowing a 240-terabyte sequencing project of PacBio data with high-speed network nodes to be processed with 1,000 megabyte memory units of a high-end supercomputer in just over three seconds

We investigate a logistic delay equation derived from a delayed Hill function with an equilibrium set to zero, where both variables represent cellular entities (e.g., onc and anti-onc proteins), and the interaction delay corresponds to production timeframes. By analyzing a parameter identified through biological data, we determine that the only admissible long-term dynamics are either convergence of all cells’ concentrations to a stable state or occurrence of oscillatory behavior via oscillatory stable limit cycles. We also identify a biological parameter capable of triggering this oscillatory response.

Statistical depth offers a unified approach to measuring centrality and centrality for various data types, including multivariate time series and point patterns. The authors introduce an Isometric Log-Ratio Depth specifically designed for these processes by integrating the concept of convexity inherent to the Log-Ratio space. The study further establishes conditions required for consistent estimation during finite sample scenarios and demonstrates computational methods for this new index when observations exist within a constrained observation window on the real timeline. Beyond this, the analysis explores regressing this depth measure against external covariates observed within that framework using a log-gamma framework to maintain covariance positive definiteness. The approach's efficacy and robustness are validated across the proposed procedure's simulation analyses, with practical applicability demonstrated through real-world datasets regarding financial returns and train arrivals, all adhering to their respective positive-defining structural constraints.

Quantum hybrid algorithms are designed to harness the distinct strengths of different quantum hardware types by integrating them. This work introduces an new model—a quantum annealing coupled system consisting of one main annealer supported by two two-qubit hybrid machines based on quantum circuits connected to it via coupling mechanisms. Analytic results on the system's stability show that stability increases with higher annealing speed when driven by a specific set of parameters selected according to a proposed strategy. Speed and the overall structure are further confirmed through a numerical investigation into Grover's search algorithm performance. Results indicate that our derived hybrid architecture proves to be particularly effective at amplifying the speed of Grover searches compared prior standalone implementations in terms of both success probabilities. These findings demonstrate the potential for our hybrid design to improve the efficiency.

This article presents a new method for achieving high-precision, short-lived nuclear mass measurements through the use of ion cyclotron resonance. By operating the ion cyclotron resonance frequency relative to a highly accurate optical frequency comb locked to optical lattice atoms, a precision significantly superior to traditional Penning trap techniques can be realized. We present the first such measurement involving exotic nuclei: an isotope mass measurement of ¹⁰⁷I at the University of Washington's Isotope Mass Separation Facility. Furthermore, the study introduces the concept of $B$-field-synchronized (isochronous) ¹⁰⁷I mass measurement, where the magnetic field is tuned to match ¹⁰⁷I's natural cyclotron frequency within this new apparatus—specifically one equipped with a magnetic field sensor for real-time monitoring of field variations—to a precision ¹⁰⁷I relative uncertainty of ²·⁷×10^(-¹⁰)—the highest achievable at the University of Washington's ISOLDE facility—and we also explore the potential for extending this method to measure nuclear structure near the nuclear structure limits at major national laboratories like CERN and Brookhaven National Laboratory.

We investigate the application of regular expressions to improve the speed and precision of recognizing structured text by providing bias. Our findings demonstrate this approach works best in two distinct regimes: a coarse-grained regime, where regular expressions bias a pre-trained Optical Character Recognition system, and a fine-grained regime, where they enable the end-to-end training of specialized recognition models. While the initial coarse-grained method yields meaningful performance gains, utilizing models trained specifically for structured text in the fine-grained approach surpasses the coarse solution and even outperforms state-of-the-art models dedicated to structured text recognition.

For a dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 174 inverse femtobarns collected at sqrt(s) = sqrt(s[NN]) = 8.16 TeV by the CMS experiment at the LHC, this study presents the inaugural observation in proton-lead collisions of a specific final state involving a high-pseudrapidity top quark. This analysis examines the final state characterized by a high-transverse-momentum lepton and high-transverse-momentum jets (specifically eight jets) showing at least one with large mass, reconstructed using jets arising primarily from c hadrons. The observed cross-section for proton-lead collisions yielding a final state with a high-transverse-momentum lepton and eight jets showing at least one large mass is measured as 3.43 inverse terabarns. This observation significantly enhances the capability to investigate the kinematic regions defined here, particularly the extraction of top-quark mass and flavor-tagging efficiency with higher precision. Furthermore, this result enables more thorough scrutiny of the underlying physics, including more precise tests of perturbative QCD predictions alongside more rigorous examinations of potential phenomena originating from quantum chromodynamic processes in proton-lead interactions.

This paper proposes an auxiliary task-driven, end-to-end approach for cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing, designed to enhance representation learning and generate more accurate SQL queries. Unlike previous methods, which design separate models to transfer text embeddings and then distinct models to generate SQL—resulting in weak alignment between generated natural language and the corresponding SQL schema—our framework features two integrated, sequential components: (1) a natural language generation task that produces intermediate representations to form the basis for semantic parsing, and (2) a text-to-SQL generation task that converts these representations into final SQL statements. By introducing this auxiliary task to create a refined semantic bridge, the model effectively transfers domain-specific knowledge and improves overall performance. Empirical evaluations on the OpenSQL and Spider datasets demonstrate that we improve state-of-the-art results across two key metrics: the top-1 Exact Match (EM) accuracy rises from 41.0% to 44.6% on OpenSQL, and execution accuracy on Cross-Domain Subqueries within the Top-10 SQL statements jumps from 60.4% to 65.4% on the Spider benchmark.

The high-dimensional rank lasso (HDR LASSO) offers an efficient solution for high-dimensional data analysis, having been introduced as a robust, outlier-resistant successor to traditional LASSO. Because of its convex formulation, it is well-suited for applications in high-dimensional robust regression, classification, and regression. Omitting the constraints on the sign, these methods allow for innovative properties. However, due to the increasing number of parameters, they are computationally expensive for current systems. We propose a new method to solve this problem, which adapts the parameter space and introduces a thresholding technique for it. Results indicate this approach is highly effective, reducing the dimensionality of the problem while preserving the desired properties. Furthermore, it outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms, as demonstrated by our theoretical analysis showing that it converges to the global minimum under mild assumptions about the data distribution. Numerical experiments confirm that it significantly outperforms comparable approaches for solving the high-dimensional rank lasso problem.

Over the last ten years, AI and data science have been adopted across the AI community to address the pressing challenges of a changing planet, with a focus on the benefits and drawbacks of these AI-based environmental solutions. This study measures the potential positive impact of such AI applications on the environment, but also uncovers their potential negative contributions, specifically by analyzing both their efficacy and environmental costs. Consequently, this work provides a reference point to guide the responsible deployment of AI in the sector, ensuring that these technologies, which are now so pervasive, continue to be a net benefit for the planet, especially in their efforts to protect the incredible diversity of the natural world, including the assessments made on the various ecosystems.

Prescriptive monitoring approaches offer higher-level intervention suggestions for ongoing cases than their monitoring counterparts do following completion. Although research into ongoing prescriptive monitoring has grown recently and covers many topics, this area still faces numerous open questions. Research teams and practitioners must collaboratively address these challenges, and the following article offers a structure for categorizing and organizing these unresolved issues. We offer a prescriptive monitoring taxonomy to clarify the subject's scope, identify knowledge gaps from both field coverage and clarity, and structure these challenges into a step-by-step research agenda.

A subset of the surface of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is subjected to heating. The task involves computing the temperature distribution over $\Omega$ and $Opt(\Omega)$ simultaneously. An optimality system is constructed involving a Boussines-type equation for thermal expansion and an optimization framework. A numerical approach utilizing Backward-Euler time discretization and finite element methods for spatial resolution employs an adaptive strategy for error management. This technique automatically identifies necessary mesh refinement to ensure reproducible results across different initial starting points and to rapidly converge to a local solution of the optimization problem.

Kernelization has emerged as a central area of study within parameterized algorithms, evolving a set of robust techniques capable of handling numerous graph problems. Although much of this success stems from problems solvable using kernelization methods rooted in modular decomposition, such an approach is not universally applicable. We address a broader and more general query: what are the most extensive classes of modifiers applicable to specific problem domains? Focusing on packing problems involving graphs, we present a unified framework that reveals a wider scope of modification possibilities. This approach also offers a methodical process for identifying problems that are most promising for effective kernelization strategies.

This paper investigates the intertwined mechanisms shaping individual opinions and social networks. We develop a framework where agents interact within groups to form both small-world networks and maintain groups of varying sizes, acknowledging that interaction ranges are constrained by a confidence level in this distance-based model. We further introduce a preference-driven perspective: when agents encounter contrasting views, they deliberately modify their own beliefs to align with a chosen viewpoint. Our contributions include a novel approach to simultaneously model network topology and opinion dynamics that accounts for these bounded confidence limits and active preferences. We analyze how these factors jointly influence opinion diffusion and the emergence of polarized communities or clusters of similar beliefs. Finally, several model parameters are examined to assess their influence on the final opinion distribution and the characteristics resulting network structure.

This work explores the interior structure of a newly identified family of asymptotically flat, charged black holes, which develop charged scalar hair when the charge-to-mass ratio is increased. Within the event horizon, the geometry mirrors an interior resembling a holographic superconductor. Notably, the system exhibits phenomena similar to Josephson oscillations within the scalar field, and the ultimate Kasner-type singularity shows extreme sensitivity to black hole parameters at high values of charge-to-mass ratio. Additionally, we identify a phase transition marking the end of scalar hair stability, corresponding to a discontinuous alteration in the metric, and we map out the complete evolution of scalar hair throughout the black hole's lifetime.

Although genes with delays in transcription initiation typically start synthesis later and yield fewer transcripts compared to genes without such delays, this study removes transcription initiation as the dominant delay factor. We introduce a computational framework that captures the entire lifecycle of RNA transcription, specifically targeting the progression from gene initiation to nuclear export or degradation. By applying this modeling approach, we identify distinct patterns of RNA production lag associated with genes with delayed initiation. These delays can range from the standard, and these genes produce similar levels of transcripts compared to those without delays.

Furthermore, we propose a multisensory detection methodology capable of handling the intrinsic asynchronicity between 2D video and 3D auditory perspectives from surveillance equipment. This paper introduces a method for generating synthetic data to analyze the impact of power crisis-induced power outages on consumer electricity usage patterns in Venezuela. Utilizing synthetic data offers a dual advantage: it prevents sensitive real information leaks and ensures safe processing against potential system failures originating from data inaccuracies. The study examines granular, hourly consumption data spanning three years (2016–2018), covering both pre-crisis periods and the crisis years of 2017 and partway through 2018. To maximize the utility of these synthetic datasets for business analysts relying on dataset-centric queries—specifically those focused on dates within the 2016–2018 range, power usage intensity, and household demographics—we employ advanced machine learning techniques. The proposed methodology is rigorous: it begins by defining an error metric optimized through the iterative resampling of a data generator, employing iterative synthetic generation combined with the Bayesian Optimization method for parameter tuning, and concludes by evaluating the analytic indistinguishability between real and synthetic datasets through the replication of data patterns. Finally, we replicate specific business analytics queries to demonstrate how synthetic data can provide acceptable results for practical applications.

Personalization of web search remains a relatively underexplored issue in news and scientific reporting. Since search results are tailored to individual users, a user may fail to encounter information they would otherwise find useful. Research has already raised concerns, yet these findings lack the benefit of empirical verification. Our work provides the first empirical study on the empirical consequences of search engine personalization. We did so using a controlled, user-study approach combined with log analysis. Results reveal that personalization causes users to overlook relevant content, while the specific personalization algorithm employed influences which information is obscured. Furthermore, we developed and released an open- sourced toolkit for personalization, named \textit{personalse}, to facilitate future research in this domain.

Program synthesis involves writing code that satisfies both a provided specification and input-output examples. Research from a human-in-the-loop setting indicates that programmers can effectively synthesize code by interpreting flow chart diagrams; they do so by understanding each diagram component and the transitions between them individually. Building on this, we introduced GRCNN, a deep convolutional neural network designed to autoencode graph images representing flow charts into structured code. While initial experimental results suggest grcnn achieves a 52% success rate in generating correct programs compared to a baseline of 0%, synthesis depends on correctly mapping both nodes and edges. To investigate failures, we developed an Edges Recognition Convolutional Network (ERCNN) to serve as an encoder and established a new end-to-end synthesis framework. This new system significantly improved accuracy to 83%. Additionally, we released the FlowNet dataset and open-source GRCNN code and models to foster further progress in program synthesis.

We explore an ensemble of techniques, some existing and others potential candidates suited for linking climate model simulations at varying scales. These methods, motivated by the need to bridge gaps between detailed high-resolution simulations and reduced-order models designed for both enhanced understanding and operational efficiency. The review encompasses model order reduction through proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and stochastic Galerkin approaches, spatial reduction strategies such as POD and the coarse modeling framework, as well several scales reduction methods including multiscale modeling, singular perturbation theory, asymptotic analysis, and homogenization.

Federated learning enables distributed training of machine learning models by allowing multiple parties to share local model parameters while keeping private data local, yet parameter exchanges can inadvertently leak sensitive information. Furthermore, they place a heavy computational burden on participants by requiring all local data to be uploaded for remote model inference. This work introduces Flatee, a framework designed for federated learning within TEEs that facilitates rapid and privacy-secure data sharing. By adapting the recently proposed "first-by-last" sharing technique, it ensures that the model remains in the TEE while the data remains local. To overcome dependencies on fully trusted nodes often present in FHE implementations, our approach minimizes risks in practical deployments. Additionally, it addresses potential manipulations during record exchange by integrating verification mechanisms such as Private Differential Privacy (PDP) and a consistency check known as Wally. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 and Clothing14 datasets demonstrate that Flatee achieves convergence rates comparable to traditional federated learning and achieves communication speeds 100 times faster than prior state-of-the-art solutions.

We also suggest that the interactions between a system, a computer, and natural randomness can be modeled using Multi-Agent Systems (MAS). Standard projection predictive inference swaps a reference model with a simpler one by projecting coefficients, yet it ignores projecting induced latent variables, thereby limiting cross-model inference for latent structures. We introduce an extension of projection predictive inference capable of handling this scenario. By constructing a projection distribution that considers both coefficient and induced latent space variables via a two-step approximation strategy, our method dynamically selects information from a reference model. Specifically, we approximation the joint posterior distribution in the projection model first via marginalization over the latent variables, second via model selection. This yields a probabilistic framework for projecting latent variables that preserves projected coefficients simultaneously. Finally, we demonstrate via simulations and real-world applications using the projection distribution derived through latent space variables, the authors can perform inference on a simpler model while retaining a high proportion of the information from more complex reference models.

Deep learning networks have proven effective across numerous tasks, including image recognition and spam detection, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks that subtly modify inputs to deceive models, such as altering spam to appear as legitimate messages. This research introduces a novel category, the model-based man-in-the-middle attack, which targets known neural network architectures. In this scenario, with limited access only to data exiting the classifier, an adversary corrupts the feature representations generated by the network to mislead subsequent layers into incorrect predictions. The attacker employs generative adversarial networks (GANs) designed to produce deceptive intermediate features, often achieving higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art baseline algorithms, a vulnerability which poses significant risks to systems using black-box or partially known convolutional convoluted networks.

A significant challenge in climate communication is the widespread presence of conspiracy theories. This study examines dominant conspiracy narratives within an extensive Twitter dataset, utilizing advanced stance detection techniques to determine if these narratives are predominantly spread by skeptics or supporters of climate action. The research identifies specific conspiracy theories' relative popularity and investigates variations in engagement based on individual beliefs about reality. Results indicate that climate skeptics are the primary drivers behind messages containing conspiracy theories. Specifically, deniers overwhelmingly dominate the discourse around the "global warming hoax" narrative, whereas messages related to the "bill Gates control agenda" appear more balanced between pro-climate activists and deniers. Finally, the study confirms that conspiracy theory content receives significantly greater engagement, measured in retweets and likes, compared to non-conspiracy information.

Learning complex tasks involving multi-agent interactions, such as those between humans and robots, poses significant challenges to both artificial intelligence and psychology. Social media generates millions of comments and posts about virtually any topic, making it difficult for scholars to discern opinions on contentious topics like climate change. Although the persistence of informed debate online presents a challenge to societal progress, this study demonstrates that structural patterns underlying polarized debates can be identified and harnessed to develop effective interventionist strategies. By positioning themselves within these underlying structures, climate researchers can optimize the impact of their communication. Specifically, we propose using social networks and influence maximization techniques to target posts effectively. To ensure our approach respects the inherent polarization of the online debate, our framework explicitly incorporates the partisan structure of social networks as a crucial factor. Empirical results show that post-targeting significantly outperforms random targeting by approximately 5% in anticipated reach and by about 11% in estimated climate-specific engagement. Importantly, compared to prior work, this research is pioneering in recognizing and accounting for the inherent partisan topology of social networks when defining and calculating reach and engagement.

Identifying active discussions regarding local or global events using real-time social media is a major, yet unsolved, challenge. Most current methods face barriers because they rely on heavy heuristics, rely on historical data to build and maintain a complex tag similarity vocabulary, and rely on on-the-fly re-assignment of relevant information, making them inflexible and ill-suited to the volatile, high-volume nature of the social web. By contrast, our approach operates in real-time and uses no historical data while spatially and temporally detecting events through direct graph analysis of geotagged posts. We represent these posts via a user interest network constructed on explicit tagging and then employ spatial-temporal subgraph extraction and clustering to discover event clusters. Experiments using more than four million real Twitter posts from the 2011 Japan Earthquake demonstrate that our system outperforms previous systems by discovering events faster and with greater accuracy.

We investigate the impact of hyperspectral pixel subtraction techniques using Independent Component Analysis (ICA), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Sparse Principal Component Analysis (S-PCA). A diverse range of classifiers—including Bayesian, k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and various Neural Network (NN) architectures—are examined after dimensionality reduction. Results indicate that IAc, when applied with fewer components, enhances classification accuracy. Specifically, reducing the dimensionality from 224 to just 10 dimensions via either Bayesian or k-NN models raised average classification scores by 4.52% and 2.38%, respectively. Interestingly, similar reduction parameters yielded poorer outcomes with the Bayesian model, whereas expanding the reduced dimension from 5 to 7 via the same approach improved results by 2.8%, highlighting nuanced dependencies on specific learning algorithms. Additionally, analysis across diverse network structures revealed that NNs respond differently to data compression; an Autoencoder achieved the highest performance with IAc on 5 dimensions, outperforming other neural configurations and even the k-NN model in this context.

Although deep neural networks excel at modeling natural language, their heavy computational demands hinder practical deployment. While classic compression techniques for these models are well-established, their application must often be evaluated alongside modern methods designed specifically for neural networks. This work reviews a wide array of both traditional andNeural-network-specific compression strategies, establishing a unified framework to aid future research. Notably, our evaluation reveals that applied individually, various recent methods fail to surpass the compression ratios achieved by several established basets. Furthermore, individual implementations of state-of-the-art methods are frequently incompatible with one another, preventing their combined use for higher model compression. Consequently, there is clearly an urgent need for joint training algorithms that can optimally compress diverse network architectures simultaneously.

This study introduces ProCS, a novel tool designed for the conformational validation and refinement of proteins. ProPT leverages quantum mechanics to calculate the chemical shifts (δₐ/δᵦ) for protein amide protons based on specific conformers, creating a database for comparison. The root of this tool's efficacy lies in its ability to non-redundantly probe the three-dimensional structure's effect on these shifts. Demonstrating the method's power, we show that only a single type of amide proton shift is sufficient to reliably distinguish between structurally distinct conformations.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator arises from the condensation of particle-hole pairs induced by lattice distortions. Applying the newly developed method, the energy gap between the valence and conduction bands in TiSe$_2$ was computed to be approximately $0.15$ eV at zero temperature. Ultimately, these discoveries inform a framework modeling the interactions, with applications ranging from detecting irregular patterns to identifying and resolving flaws in current triage methodologies.

This work evaluates the effectiveness of coupling ozone and ultraviolet (UV) light in gas-phase reactors to oxidize pollutants in flue gases, specifically targeting the reduction of sulfur dioxide (SO₂) through numerical simulations of a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR). We integrated experimental data on the ozone UV-photon flux with theoretical models of radiation transport to construct a two-dimensional reactor model. Results indicate that simultaneously applying UV-ozone is a viable method for cleaning air and flue gas, yielding higher pollutant removal than using ozone alone. By optimizing the positions of UV lamps within the reactor, removal efficiencies reach approximately 90% for H₂S and 85.58% for SO₂.

The deployment of Machine Learning in practice frequently presents challenges, such as reliance on opaque models, uncertainty stemming from imperfect sensor data, and the limitation of outputting a deterministic class label instead of a probabilistic distribution. Addressing these issues, this paper proposes Indecision Trees—a variation of traditional Decision Trees that handles inference under uncertainty. Unlike standard models, Indecision trees produce a robust distribution across potential labels and can be deconstructed into actionable logical arguments for integration into other reasoning frameworks.

Time series analysis relies heavily on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for tasks ranging from similarity measurement to relatedness search; however, DTW's quadratic complexity has historically restricted its use to very short sequences. Although Complete Matching was recently suggested to handle similar efficiency challenges in the sorted context of time series analysis, its complexity remains prohibitive for the general case involving arbitrary time series. In response to these challenges, this study introduces Pruned DTW (Pruned DTW), a technique that leverages a convex-helloshaped constraint to prematurely terminate calculations. By establishing the Shifting Windows property and defining a new cost envelope derived from such a shape, this approach enables algorithms to discard unnecessary nodes in the time warping dynamic table significantly earlier than previously possible methods allow. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this technique can abandon up to 90 percent of computations across datasets, achieving speedups of as much as two orders of magnitude.

Current testing assessment tools generally lack the capacity to interact with learners, support individual progress, or provide real-time performance insights. Although researchers recognize interactive feedback as a viable response to these limitations, empirical studies comparing the specific impacts of different feedback teaching styles remain scarce. To address this need, we compared inquiry-based conceptual feedback (IBCF) with traditional detailed feedback (TF) within a Software Testing process, utilizing a large-scale empirical study. Conducted across ten university classes, the study involved 213 participants who underwent either an IBCF-based or TF-based instructional approach for basic software testing over several weeks, followed by assessments of their problem-solving skills and self-regulated learning abilities. Our findings indicate that while both feedback approaches yield positive results in addressing testing tasks and promoting conceptual learning, IBCF produces superior outcomes for both software problem-solving and the development of the specific testing concepts it targets.

We detail each component and their synergistic relationship within an expressive framework. Furthermore, we designed a user-centric approach that leverages this potential and evaluated the proposed system through a real-world case study.

Over-smoothing represents a critical challenge restricting the effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks. Although prior studies have explored these issues, the root mechanisms remain insufficiently defined. This paper investigates the theoretical mechanisms of the over-smoothing effect within Graph Convolutional Networks. Specifically, drawing inspiration from heat diffusion, we reframe graph convolution operators and analyze their characteristics. By examining the characteristics of these operators, we establish that standard graph convolution operators inherently possess positive and symmetric properties, enabling them to be interpreted as discrete, continuous-time symmetric diffusion maps, thereby offering new insights into the graph learning framework. A continuous analysis framework grounded in Graph Self-adjoint Operator Algebra further illuminates the mechanisms of graph learning and over-smoothing. By leveraging the spectral theory of continuous-time symmetric diffusion maps and our findings, we demonstrate that the graph convolution process functions as an isometric transformation that continuously approaches an ideal diffusion map, with this convergence occurring in the graph self-adjoint operator topology. Specifically, we prove that as iterations increase, both the graph convolution layers and their weights converge toward those of an ideal diffusion map, with weights approaching a stochastic adjacency matrix and weights' coefficients approaching 1. These theoretical findings facilitate a deeper comprehension and offer practical suggestions for graph learning models designed to circumvent the over-smoothing limitation.

This study represents the inaugural experimental assessment of the standard assumption of credibility in the second-price auction mechanism, a assumption that relies on the premise of no incentive to bid above true valuation because the highest losing bid results in paying the runner-up price, not the bidder's own offer. Evidence suggests this assumption fails to hold in reality, potentially causing bidders to overstate values despite the mechanism's design. To test this, researchers conducted auctions incorporating verifiable but privately known overhead costs to create opportunities for strategic overbidding. After conducting over 12,000 second-price auctions across more than 3,000 participants—acquired via an online survey over two periods—researchers analyzed bidding behaviors. Results confirm significant overbidding, indicating true preference reveals are replaced by flawed judgments of the auction format rather than credible strategies. Specifically, more individuals overbid during period 2, following period 1 experiences, compared to period 1. Furthermore, the distribution and magnitude of these overbids varied significantly based on gender, age range and other demographic factors.

We further investigate the entropy - temperature relationships as well as the equation - of - state parameters to assess the nature of the cosmological horizon. These considerations demonstrate that $f(I_T)$ gravitation provides a viable theoretical alternative for describing early cosmological evolution.

Academic researchers acquire a broad repertoire of domain-specific information, such as identifying appropriate methodologies for manuscript preparation or publishing in high-impact venues. While peer support and internet searches are commonly utilized, questions focused on information seeking within scholarly articles have received little attention. Our contribution addresses this gap through the creation of ISQA, a comprehensive dataset of academic information-seeking queries paired with accurate answer sets. Developed in collaboration with master's and Ph.D. students across three computer science programs, ISQA comprises 3,888 question-answer pairs across 948 academic papers. The dataset's unique architecture features multiple possible answers for each query, reflecting the valid range of responses often found in scholarly literature. Each entry further details the specific information需求 behind the question. To validate its utility, we established a prototypical application demonstrating how academic information seeking can be automated utilizing our ISQA.

Results confirm that the FAB method introduces significant issues with such simulations. Medical notes serve as extensive repositories of historical patient records, yet ICD codes offer structured representations of specific clinical events found within these texts, such as diagnoses or treatments. Although Natural Language Processing (NLD) techniques can extract such structured information, they generally suffer from generalization challenges and a high demand for annotated labels. This paper proposes an iterative algorithm for deriving time-dependent data for numerical evolutions within numerical relativity. Traditional methods face challenges generating future light cone conditions regarding boundary stress-energy and directional derivatives of the extrinsic curvature that their corresponding initial data methods do not accommodate. Leveraging recent findings regarding the solvability of these light cone conditions, our method operates by repeatedly applying a shrink-shrink strategy to contract asymptotically flat spacetimes with spherical topologies. The principal aim of the JUNO experiment is to resolve neutrino mass hierarchy using a 20-kiloton liquid scintillator sphere, the network of which will link the mainland of China and the island of the same name. A defining requirement of this project involves calibrating the large-scale detection volumes using uniform performance from more than twenty thousand 20-inch photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). To fulfill these demands, a specialized quality control framework has been established to ensure that all photomultiplier tubes exhibit consistent sensitivity and photoelectron production. In this study, an initial batch comprising fifteen 20-inch PMT units underwent comprehensive evaluation. This involved a high-precision gain measurement utilizing a multi-stage statistical method grounded in laboratory-based LED performance tests, supplemented by detailed physical inspections and chemical analyses. This report outlines the small-scale testing procedures employed and presents further research required to scale the process for the production lines involved in JUNO's instrumentation.

Predicting multidimensional time series is a vital yet difficult challenge across various domains. Even with advances in machine learning and deep learning models, this task remains difficult because it necessitates analyzing interactions across multiple dimensions and capturing long-range temporal dependencies that are both temporal and multidimensional. Although many existing methods exist, recent studies indicate an underrepresentation of graph-based approaches. To address this gap, we present AGCN, a novel adaptive multidimensional time series prediction framework built on graph convolutional networks. This model treats time series data as node time series within the graph and innovatively transforms the problem to include predicting the interactions (edges) between nodes. Furthermore, we develop a dual-stage network: using local temporal patterns from individual univariate series in the first stage to identify significant long-term dependencies in the second. To optimize the framework, we propose a new variational autoencoder (VAE) capable of reconstructing both the multidimensional time series and the graph structure simultaneously, ensuring effective interaction learning. Validation against the popular Multivariate/Missing Dataset (MTM) benchmark demonstrates that AGCN surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The code will be made public at [https://github.com/zhangziziz/AGCN].

Dispersion is a critical parameter in optical characterisation and on-sky performance testing, particularly within a ground-based environment where light travels through the atmosphere before reaching the telescope instruments. Since this atmospheric journey is complex, scientific models are employed to approximate it; however, the specific atmospheric model used has the potential to introduce errors during measurement. This study aims to assess the quality of standard atmospheric models by comparing them against direct on-sky observations of dispersion obtained using the IMACS instrument at the 1.9m Jean-Baptiste Lamotte telescope. Using on-sky data, we characterised three key parameters of the atmosphere: its vertical structure, the dispersion per atmospheric layer, and the total vertical measurement uncertainty, achieving a resolution of 10 cm. This direct measurement profile serves as a benchmark for existing models. We propose a method to fit various atmospheric models against these observations and apply this approach to characterize a standard atmospheric model, such as the Molodern, using observational data. The research also examined how observational errors propagate into the derived model parameters, revealing a delicate correlation between these variables that makes their determination highly sensitive and difficult.

Pre-trained language models have emerged as vital components of recent ranking systems, yielding remarkable performance. Knowledge distillation serves as the key strategy to sustain such high performance with efficient computation. Our work centers on two fundamental problems in creating knowledge distillations for ranking: effectively aggregating information from multiple teachers and incorporating label information throughout the distillation process. Addressing these challenges simultaneously with a unified approach called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which iteratively ensembles logits from various teachers under label supervision, has proven successful. Our experiments, covering both offline and online settings, show competitive outcomes, and this method is now live in a commercial search system.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) can be represented by hypothetical light scalar or vector fields that couple minimally to the standard model. These fields are theorized to behave as classical, oscillating fields with frequencies determined by their masses (approximately $m/2\hbar$). If a classical cube contains multiple such particles, they could generate oscillating charge fluctuations at distinct frequencies, which could, after normalization, be detected as temporal correlations. Since BDM densities are so low, these correlations likely fall below current detector noise. By integrating the signal from many independent experiments, however, one can amplify these correlations by an order of magnitude proportional to the number of sources. This paper outlines how to utilize these correlations to identify and constrain UBDM, using examples from $\phi^3$ scalar theories and U(1) gauge theories.

This study investigates a one-to-one dimensional torus continuous-domain basis pursuit formulation. We analyze the problem's duality, establish an equivalence between it and the total variation denoising problem introduced by Beck and Tsur (2014), and investigate the problem's sensitivity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that uniqueness is not a guaranteed property. Lastly, we introduce a penalty-transformed basis pursuit problem and prove an upper limit for its smoothness, which supports lower bounds indicating that uniqueness is not universal in the original problem.

In finite element simulations of fluid dynamics, vector-valued quantities like velocity and momentum are frequently represented using Raviart-Thomas elements. To achieve second-order accuracy for these vector fields, a typical approach employs linear elements for the finite element method's vector transport equation. However, the standard $C^0$ piecewise linear method yields only first-order convergence due to a discrepancy between the strong and weak formulations of this transport equation. This issue can be resolved by introducing a correction term to the discrete weak formulation. Drawing from a novel analysis of the relationship among various numerical methods for vector transport—specifically finite volume, gradient recovery, and semi-discrete approaches—we derive modified algorithms that restore second-order accuracy. These methods have been implemented in two- and three-dimensional settings for free-surface shallow water equations using rectangular and triangular meshes. Experimental results confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed corrections.

While Shannon entropy and associated metrics like mutual information are fundamental, their estimation from finite datasets remains the Bayesian evidence (or marginal likelihood)—a challenge primarily addressed using entropy sampling. This study examines whether the Nested Sampling algorithm, renowned for its efficiency in calculating Bayesian evidence, can also estimate entropies and mutual information. We demonstrate through simulations that Nested Sampling calculates these quantities more rapidly than Monte Carlo sampling and demonstrates better or comparable accuracy to grid-based methods. Additionally, we find it offers superior flexibility and robustness in handling high-dimensional data compared to grid-based approaches. Thus, we conclude Nested Sampling is effective for estimating entropies and mutual information while maintaining its role in evidence computation.

This paper investigates the solvability of a nonlinear, strictly convex (with piecewise $C^{1}$ derivative), first-order hyperbolic conservation law featuring localized discontinuities in the source term. It introduces and analyzes solvability when boundaries meet source discontinuities, defining both classical and weak measure-valued solutions via a Lax-Pitgarden-type variational approach. Uniqueness is established for these weak solutions, while continuous dependence on initial data follows for trajectories whose support has finite measure. Finally, a proof demonstrates that trajectories generated by this proposed scheme converge toward the solution corresponding to continuously perturbed boundaries, effectively showing a robust limit under high-frequency source variations.

With Internet of Things (IoT) devices becoming increasingly ubiquitous and a diverse array of attacks evolving rapidly, analyzing traffic from low-specification devices under strict security and resource constraints is a challenging yet essential task. Relying heavily on the Naive Bayed algorithm for traffic analysis while encoding raw data into two specialized features, the system conserves both computational resources and transmission bandwidth. Our experimental results demonstrate that this efficient classification approach maintains satisfactory accuracy, operating within minimal memory, time, and bandwidth limits.

This article examines the Schreier growth bounds for actions of groups that are both solvable and finitely generated. Furthermore, we establish the existence of uniform bounds on exponential growth constants and the orders of associated normal subgroups relative to the group's generating sets. Finally, we outline several examples involving $\mathbb{Z}^k$-actions on graphs and XG sets within these three distinct categories of action development.

Modern machine learning and statistical analysis have significantly advanced the field of physics-information extraction from experiments and simulations. Contemporary approaches also seek to derive universal laws, even in the presence of noise; these methods often employ smoothness-based regularization for function approximation. Since anomalies often result from genuine scientific discoveries, the framework for detecting them intersects closely with physics model inference. This review explores state-of-the-century methodologies for discovering physical insights, the intrinsic link between anomaly detection and inference, and how smoothness regularization facilitates identifying universal laws.

Inelastic neutron scattering not only facilitates the measurement of a dynamic structure factor—imaging 1-D diffusion—but also enables access to the van Hove correlation function, $S(q, \omega)$. The feature known as the boson peak (BP), arising in many glassy materials, is identified as the mid-infrared minimum within this function at low wavevector ($q$). When scrutinized in detail, the BP is not a true peak but a valley, which diminishes in visibility as $q$ increases. This behavior is comprehensible through the asymptotic limit of $S(q, \omega)$ for small $q$, demonstrating that in diffusives 1-D processes, the intensity remains $q$-independent at the highest frequencies (the so-called "white noise" regime). Consequently, the apparent valley is an inevitable outcome of normalizing scattering intensity by $q$, which creates a bottleneck regardless of the specific diffusion mechanism, whether random walk, jump, or continuous. This analysis is confirmed across multiple 1-D systems, including liquid protium and deuterium, various protic ionic liquids, and multiple eutectic nitrate nitrate glasses.

The three-dimensional stable roommates problem involves matching members of two cohorts on two streets that intersect at a corner, resulting in the formation of stable ordered pairs of pairs. Currently regarded as the sole practical pathway for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing, the surface code relies on rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling experimentally observed faulty syndrome measurements. This paper demonstrates that decoding under fully realistic fault-tolerant constraints can be elegantly restructured as iterative interactions between a decoding agent and its code environment, thereby allowing reinforcement learning techniques to develop effective agents specifically for decoding. Employing deep q-learning, we illustrate this method by training high-speed decoding algorithms tailored to the surface code across multiple noise scenarios.

Quantum metrology leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance measurement precision. This abstract introduces a method utilizing a dipole-coupled network of two cavities, where a targeted quantum dipole interaction between them enables an exceptionally accurate determination of the dipole's coupling strength via a counting scheme based on quantum jumps observed in dipole occupation numbers. Although networks with abundant features and detailed representations often yield superior models, their training frequently suffers from generalization issues, a phenomenon we term the "optimization-generalization dilemma." This conflict arises because the complex loss landscapes created by detailed representations lead to local minima that offer inadequate generalization. To address this, we introduce RFC-OGD, a method designed to mitigate these issues. The approach decouples the demanding backpropagation-driven training from generalization-focused data sampling, achieving this by modifying data sampling strategies. By doing so, RFC-OGD simplifies the loss landscape, enabling more effective backpropagation training while still producing superior models. Empirical results confirm the efficacy and efficiency of this approach, demonstrating significant reductions in local minima prevalence alongside performance improvements across various real-world datasets.

Meta-analyses often incorporate data from multiple studies, involving numerous effect size estimates that serve as the primary outcome. This study introduces a multi-time-step algorithm designed to improve computational efficiency in particle-resolved simulations. This study examines how incompressible fluid turbulence interacts with finite temperature effects and thermal fluctuations. The analysis begins with the basic conservation laws and applies the coarse-graining technique to derive the equations governing turbulence at scales where dissipation occurs. This process results in the averaged equations featuring the Riemann invariant formulation of the Riemann conservation laws, supplemented by a stochastic term that represents thermal noise. This stochastic contribution arises directly from fluctuating heat currents and temperature variations within a coarse view, and their magnitude aligns with equilibrium noise predictions given by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Furthermore, the temperature fluctuations gradually diminish as the Reynolds number decreases. The resulting deterministic equations contain significantly lower energy than those defining mainstream inertial-range turbulence but remain distinct from the non-fluctuating Riemann-conservation formulations used in classical turbulence theory. The validity of this new framework of dissipation-range turbulence is supported by analytical solutions representing steady-state fully developed turbulence. The analysis continues with a computational analysis comparing solutions generated by the new stochastic equations against experimental observations. The simulation results accurately replicate key experimental features, specifically the decay of fluctuations as energy scales move away from the dissipation region. The study concludes by suggesting that the proposed framework for dissipation-range turbulence with incorporated thermal fluctuations could provide essential insights for understanding active turbulence.

We review available technologies and potential approaches for building astrometric systems optimized for cross-correlation techniques. These methods rely on computing the association between an observed spectrum and a reference or library spectrum to derive a correlation score. A high score implies a match to the target object derived from that reference. Because these techniques provide a more efficient and robust extraction of radial velocity data and certain elemental information compared to conventional spectral analysis, they are increasingly popular in modern astrophysics. When the input and reference spectra are similar, the resulting velocity derivations depend less on absolute wavelength calibration, offering greater robustness against spectral line shifts. For example, all current exoplanet cross-correlation findings from planetary atmospheres suffer limitations due to a limited number of identifiable spectral lines, or 'line density.' To achieve more robust atmospheric cross-correlation analyses, we require instruments that deliver higher spectral resolution and stability across the imaging field. The following discussion evaluates whether instruments such as the Wedgefield Spectrograph (WFS), which are not strictly bound by the constraints governing the cross-correlation of spectral lines, are still suitable. The answer is no, as this approach requires higher resolution and stability. We will also explore whether it is feasible to achieve these critical resolution and stability goals without compromising the planetary atmosphere analysis, or if a compromise is currently necessary.

By computing the magnitude of loss across regions of interest and using it to identify areas of poor model fit on a global scale, RANG dynamically adds nodes specifically in those underrepresented parts of the solution. Together, these improvements accelerate training velocity and successfully mitigate convergence stalls without the need for reinitialization. Our approach was validated across benchmarks including the heat equation, Advection-Diffusion model, Navier-Stokes equations, KdV, Burgers, Cimentini, Helimton-Rodriguez, Navier-Stokes and a nonlinear PDE, demonstrating robust effectiveness.

Furthermore, our analysis reveals that when surface tension variations are negligible, maximum growth rates of a liquid film on fibers occur at wavenumbers that increase with greater slip lengths. These surges can be substantially higher than those observed in no-slip conditions, thereby confirming the beneficial impact of slip in controlling such fluids.

Current speech synthesis systems face a critical challenge in producing natural-duration synthetic speech. While standard TTS models typically output speech at the standard 16,000 Hz sampling—resulting in overly short and unnatural durations—researchers have introduced deep learning techniques to synthesize speech at lower sampling rates for naturalistic timing. By continuously updating duration statistics and leveraging the deep synthesis capabilities of modern TTS, we demonstrate that middle and slow speech speeds are now achievable without the extensive training data previously required. This study validates the methodology by benchmarking against state-of-the-art sampling rates and duration-generation techniques, utilizing automatic metrics and manual evaluations from human listeners.

Laboratory experiments were conducted to examine the entrainment of the ambient fluid by an axisymmetric, turbulent, fully developed gravity-driven plume carrying finely divided solid particles. In this study, both the fluid and the settling particles contributed to momentum, while the buoyancy of the particles was considered negligible relative to that of the carrier fluid. Experimental measurements included plume dimensions, velocities, concentrations, and ratios of fluid to particle fluxes as a function of distance from the source. Observations demonstrated that the plume expands at a consistent geometric scaling, maintains a steady peak particle concentration, and exhibits constant dimensionless plume boundaries. Furthermore, the plume's width grew at a rate 1.4 times greater than that of a equivalent clear plume, whereas the velocity decayed more slowly. Consequently, the entrainment coefficient was not only a function of Plummer's Reynolds number but also exhibited dependence on the particle Froude number. Additionally, numerical simulations utilizing a model that neglects particle-induced turbulent enhancement failed to accurately replicate the observed widening of the plume.

The transmission of infectious diseases presents a significant challenge to public health, a difficulties addressed effectively by SIR epidemiological models, which typically rely on populations organized into discrete groups with uniform intergroup connection. Consequently, these classical methods fail to capture the intricate, high-order interactions inherent in society. This research generalizes SIR by utilizing spectral graph theory, focusing specifically on spectral threshold phenomena and applying the framework to hypergraphs that accommodate multi-way interactions. The study derives rigorous bounds SIR persistence, contrasting these findings with established results from standard network theory. Furthermore, the authors introduce a novel hierarchical framework, positing that spectral analysis of hypergraphs will be pivotal in understanding complex, high-order interaction systems across diverse fields such as statistical physics and machine learning.

The recent discovery of two-dimensional (2D) two-point magnetic semiconductors, combined with their inherent lattice symmetry properties, presents significant opportunities for exploring spin-orbit phenomena. In materials like CrI$_2$, magnetic moments originate directly from structural symmetry rather than being induced by it. Consequently, we employ first-order principles and spin-resolved density functional theory to analyze magnetized Iodine structures and investigate how to manipulate spin textures via external electric fields. Our findings reveal that a vertical electric field can manipulate spin textures without necessitating the breaking of inversion symmetry. Notably, while our predictions indicate the absence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction due to preserved symmetry, a Rashba spin splitting effect persists at edge states maintaining a zero net magnetization. This effect can be modulated by applied electric fields. We further examine spin textures within a ferromagnetic Flack structure, observing a unique chirality-dependent morphology characterized by multi-domain "fingers." These effects hold significant implications for advanced spintronic applications in flat magnetic systems.

Observations of cool giant stars indicate the presence of anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by equatorial regions rotating more slowly than polar areas. The present study utilizes mean-field dynamo theory to investigate how this reversed differential rotation influences magnetic cycles. Based on an axisymmetric mean-field alpha-omega model incorporating a bell-shaped alpha profile, latitudinal magnetic transport, and explicit latitudential differential rotation, we explored the parametric space to isolate the impact of reversed differential rotation by keeping other dynamical processes constant. We found that magnetic cycles driven by anti-solar differential rotation yield equatorially prominent magnetic cycles yet lack the pronounced 11-gauss symmetry break observed in the Sun. Furthermore, the magnetic cycle period under these anti-solar conditions remains largely independent of the differential rotation amplitude, mirroring solar behavior; however, unlike the solar case where greater solar differential amplitudes correlate with longer cycles and stronger cycles, differential amplitudes in this context do enhance the strength of magnetic cycles.

Multimodal deep learning aims to combine information from various unimodal inputs to enhance overall system performance. Although numerous multimodal frameworks exist, organizing them remains difficult due to their diverse architectures, optimization techniques, and information fusion methods. This paper introduces the Generalized K-Fan Multimodal Model (KKFM), which is designed to integrate data across multiple scenarios with flexible structures, effective optimization, and robust learning mechanisms. A primary contribution focuses on deriving new generative and discriminative KKFM architectures, which inherit the model's inherent advantages. Specifically, proposed methods such as the Gradient Descent Optimization-based Fused Net (GDFN) ensure efficient fusion processing, while the Gradient Descent Optimization-Separated Net (GDSN) facilitates maximum mutual information retention among distinct modalities. By extending the framework to include a multi-level loss function for multiway fusion, the proposed approach successfully addresses challenges in complex applications like multi-level facial expression recognition and multi-views classification. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that GGFM achieves superior application performance alongside the development of multiple innovative strategies.

We introduce McMini, a dominance-guided, context-independent model checker that integrates into the Mini language family to program correct algorithms for resource allocation in multi-threaded environments. By applying this algorithm within the tool, we achieve the first implementation that explicitly tracks and explores maximal runtime processes, offering significant improvements in model-checking efficiency. This study investigates a model of a general branching population featuring many alleles with arbitrary frequencies, where the conditional branching mechanism and an independent coalescent process determine the system's dynamics that together yield an approximation of the frequency spectrum. We provide the analysis required to validate this prior model, applying it specifically to branching Lyapunov populations where we converge toward a limiting frequency spectrum determined entirely by the coalescent's time scaling and the branching mechanism. We further develop an approximating algorithm that reconstructs the frequency spectrum from the system's frequency generating function.

The primary objective of spoofing detection systems is to identify synthetic artifacts embedded in speech resulting from synthesis or conversion processes. This study introduces the incorporation of attention rectified linear units (AReLU) into end-to-end detection architectures. By leveraging the attention mechanism within ARe LU to prioritize significant features, the proposed framework enhances signal relevance and filters out unnecessary data. The framework was evaluated on the Logical Access task using the 2019 IEEE AudioSPERX competition dataset. Evaluation results demonstrated that this model surpasses several baseline architectures by significantly improving the Equal Error Rate (EER) across all participating conditions.

Supergravity, a gauge theory of gravity coupled to local supersymmetry, likely represents the correct framework to describe gravity at energy scales significantly below the Planck mass and prior to achieving quantum consistency. Consequently, constructing effective field theories (EFTs) using supersymmetry should yield more reliable supersymmetric gravitational models than does taking the $\text{Planck} \to \infty$ limit, which typically decouples non-local interactions. By employing EFTs that retain low-energy remnants of a supersymmetric extension, one can derive locally supersymmetric EFTs of inflation. This work details the edge-case reduction method, demonstrating its application in generating two such inflationary EFTs by deriving their classical equations of motion and analyzing their quantum corrections.

Nonreciprocal optical systems are widely used to manipulate the signal transmission of light based on its travel direction, but in this study, we investigate a new type of nonreciprocity that manifests specifically within photon pair correlations rather than linear propagation. This phenomenon represents a reversible behavior in the second-order coherence functions of entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing on a silicon microdisk, as confirmed by both experimental and theoretical evidence. Crucially, inverting the direction of the pumping beam causes significant suppression of these coherence functions while remaining neutral to the energy transmitted by the pumps.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a prominent class of quantum computing architectures. This study examines high-resolution near-field imaging of two types of superconductantic planar microwave resonators: coplanar waveguide (CPW) resonators and stripline resonators adapted for 2-D integration. Although the impedance characteristics of these structures differ, the measured field distributions in the plane of the resonators are comparable. Specifically, the quality factors (Q) of the fundamental modes in both resonator types align closely, confirming that the Q-limiting mechanisms are essentially identical. Nevertheless, stripline resonators demonstrate approximately ten times higher performance compared to CPW resonators.
